FINA 405 · International Financial Management
FX Forwards & Futures
Lecture 6 · Fall 2026 · University of San Diego
Today: How do forward contracts and futures eliminate FX uncertainty — and when should a firm use them?
Section 1 — Bridge from Lec 5
From IRP to Forward Contracts
Interest Rate Parity doesn't just explain rates — it is the forward rate.
📌 Recall: IRP Formula
The forward rate is the no-arbitrage price — set by interest differentials, not forecasts.
📦 What is a Forward Contract?
An OTC agreement between two parties to exchange currencies at a predetermined rate on a future date.

✓ No upfront cost  |  ✓ Customizable
✓ Eliminates FX risk  |  ✗ No liquidity
Key point: The fair forward rate is exactly the IRP rate. If the market deviates — CIA arbitrage forces it back.
Section 1 — CIA Review
Covered Interest Arbitrage: The Trade
GBP/USD · Spot = 1.2500 · rUSD = 5% · rGBP = 2% · T = 1yr · Fmkt = 1.3000
Step-by-Step CIA (start with $1,000,000)
① Borrow
$1,000,000 at 5% USD
Owe $1,050,000 in 1yr
→
② Convert
$1M ÷ 1.2500
=£800,000 spot
→
③ Invest
£800K at 2% GBP
=£816,000 in 1yr
→
④ Sell fwd
£816K × 1.3000
=$1,060,800
IRP Check
FIRP = 1.2868 < Fmkt = 1.3000
→ Forward is overpriced → sell it!
✓ Arbitrage Profit
Receive: $1,060,800
Repay loan: $1,050,000
Profit = $10,800 per $1M

Section 1 — Exercise 1 Solution
CIA: The General Strategy
⚠ Complete Exercise 1 first — then review this solution!
① Identify the Mispricing
Compare Fmkt vs FIRP.

If Fmkt > FIRP → base currency is overvalued in the forward market → CIA opportunity exists.
② Execute the Trade
Borrow in the undervalued quote currency (USD, high rquote)
Invest in the overvalued base currency (rbase < rquote)
Sell base forward at inflated Fmkt
③ Collect the Profit
Profit per $1M:
= $1M × (Fmkt − FIRP) / S

Each group's Fmkt > FIRP → locked-in arbitrage.
Borrow $1M
at rquote (USD)
→
Buy base spot
$1M ÷ S
→
Invest at rbase
for T years
→
Sell fwd at Fmkt
overpriced!
→
PROFIT
Key insight: You borrow in the undervalued currency (quote/USD) and invest in the overvalued currency (base), then lock in gains by selling the base forward at an inflated price. CIA arbitrage forces Fmkt back toward FIRP.
💬 Think: How does CIA pressure drive Fmkt back to FIRP? What happens to spot rates, forward rates, and interest rates when many traders execute this simultaneously?
Section 2 — FX Instruments
FX Forward Contracts
The most common hedging tool for corporate FX exposure.
What It Is
A private, binding agreement between two counterparties to exchange a specific amount of currency at a pre-agreed rate on a future date.

▸ Traded OTC (not on an exchange)
▸ Fully customizable: amount, date, currency pair
▸ No upfront premium required
▸ Settled by physical delivery or net cash
Why Firms Use It
Exporters (receivable in foreign currency):
→ Sell the foreign currency forward — lock in USD proceeds

Importers (payable in foreign currency):
→ Buy the foreign currency forward — lock in USD cost

Multinationals: hedge known cash flows in multiple currencies simultaneously
Pricing Reminder: F = IRP Rate
Bank quotes the IRP rate. Deviation → arbitrage → rate reverts. No-arbitrage = fair price.
Section 2 — FX Instruments
FX Futures Markets
Exchange-traded standardized contracts — the public market for FX hedging.
Key Facts About FX Futures
▸ Traded on CME Group (Chicago Mercantile Exchange)
▸ Standardized contract sizes (e.g., €125,000 per EUR contract)
▸ Daily mark-to-market & margin calls
▸ Very liquid — easy to enter & exit
▸ Regulated by CFTC — transparent pricing
▸ Most contracts closed before delivery
Most Common Contracts
EUR/USD · GBP/USD · JPY/USD · CAD/USD
AUD/USD · CHF/USD · MXN/USD & more

Quoted as: USD per unit of foreign currency
CME Group — Emerging Markets FX Futures
Section 2 — FX Instruments
Forwards vs. Futures: Key Differences
Same economic purpose — very different mechanics. Choosing the right tool matters.
When to Use FORWARDS
✓ Known, specific exposure (exact amount & date)
✓ Large, customizable hedge
✓ Relationship banking (OTC)
✓ Prefer no mark-to-market cash flows
When to Use FUTURES
✓ Need liquidity — enter/exit quickly
✓ Speculate on FX direction
✓ Prefer exchange-traded transparency
✓ Standard contract size is sufficient

Section 3 — Case Study
Case Study: Caterpillar Inc.
A global machinery maker faces AUD exposure from an Australian equipment sale.
The Scenario
Caterpillar sold mining equipment to an Australian company.

Payment due in 3 months: AUD 1,000,000
Current Spot: AUD/USD = 0.6500
3M AUD Futures: 0.6400
If converted today: $650,000

Risk: AUD may depreciate before receipt → fewer USD
Caterpillar's Exposure
CAT has an AUD receivable = long AUD
FX risk hurts when AUD/USD falls

Question: Should CAT hedge?
If yes — how?
AUD/USD — Historical Rate (Yahoo Finance)
IRP Forward Rate Check
Futures at 0.64 ≈ IRP rate (rAUD≈4%, rUSD≈5.25%)
Section 3 — Case Study
Case 1: Caterpillar Does Not Hedge
Receives AUD 1M in 3 months at whatever spot rate prevails.
3M OutcomeAUD/USD SpotUSD Receivedvs. Today's Value ($650K)
🟢 AUD Appreciates0.6800$680,000+$30,000 windfall
⚪ No Change0.6500$650,000No change
🔴 AUD Depreciates0.6000$600,000−$50,000 loss vs plan
The Problem
CAT's USD revenue is completely uncertain.
Finance team cannot budget reliably.
Board cannot commit to USD earnings projections.
Suppliers, payroll contracts in USD — all at risk.
The Upside Trap
"But what if AUD goes UP?" — that's speculation, not corporate treasury.

CAT's core business is selling equipment, not taking FX positions. The upside is also the downside.
Section 3 — Case Study
Case 2: Caterpillar Hedges with AUD Futures
CAT shorts AUD/USD futures at 0.6400 — locks in $640,000 regardless of spot.
3M OutcomeSpot AUD/USDPhysical AUD RevenueFutures P&LNet USD
🟢 AUD Appreciates0.6800$680,000−$40,000$640,000 ✓
⚪ No Change0.6500$650,000−$10,000$640,000 ✓
🔴 AUD Depreciates0.6000$600,000+$40,000$640,000 ✓
✓ Perfect Hedge Result
Futures P&L = (0.64 − spot) × 1,000,000
Physical revenue = spot × 1,000,000

Net = 0.64 × 1,000,000 = $640,000
Always. Every scenario. No uncertainty.
💬 Discussion
• Is $640,000 "good"? Why or why not?
• CAT locked in $640K — but spot could end at $680K. Was hedging a mistake?
• Key insight: Hedging is about certainty, not profit.
Section 3 — Summary
Hedge vs. No Hedge: The Takeaway
❌ No Hedge (Speculative)
Revenue: $600K to $680K
Expected value ≈ $640K but highly uncertain

✗ Cannot commit to stakeholders
✗ FX risk embedded in core business
✗ Potential for large, unbudgeted losses
✓ Forward Hedge (Certain)
Revenue: $640,000 — guaranteed

✓ Certain budgeting and planning
✓ Eliminates FX from P&L volatility
✓ Focuses management on core operations
📌 Three Reasons Companies Hedge
1. Certainty
Lock in cash flows for budgeting
2. Focus
Remove FX noise from core P&L
3. Stakeholders
Reduce earnings volatility for investors

Section 4 — Summary
What We Learned Today
1
CIA is real and quantifiable. When Fmkt ≠ FIRP, covered interest arbitrage earns a riskless profit — like the $10,800 GBP/USD trade we reviewed.
2
Forwards lock in cash flows. OTC, customizable, no upfront cost. The most common corporate hedging tool for known FX exposures.
3
Futures add liquidity & standardization. Exchange-traded (CME), mark-to-market daily, but less flexible on size and maturity.
4
Hedging ≠ profit guarantee. Caterpillar locked in $640K — but certainty was the goal, not beating the market. Managing risk, not speculating.
5
Multi-currency hedging is common. NovaTech's dual hedge (EUR + GBP) shows that firms manage portfolios of FX exposures — netted or hedged leg by leg.
6
IRP is the backbone. Every forward rate and futures price you'll ever encounter is anchored to the IRP no-arbitrage condition. This is your foundation.
